claims.text: The as-deposited multilayer HEA coatings have clearly defined, coherent interfaces between alternating layers.
Coherent interfaces in multilayer HEA coatings physically impede dislocation glide.
Chemical and lattice mismatches at multilayer interfaces create local fields that hinder dislocation motion.
Interface-mediated dislocation blocking increases the activation energy for creep deformation.
The increased activation barrier enhances the creep resistance of multilayer HEA coatings.
Pronounced interfacial chemical and lattice mismatches produce stress fields and dislocation pile-ups.
Local structural and chemical disorder at multilayer interfaces raises the energy barrier for both dislocation glide and climb.
Hindering dislocation glide and climb slows the accumulation of permanent plastic strain over time.
Under matched creep conditions, multilayer HEA coatings will have lower creep rates than monolithic HEA coatings.
Under matched creep conditions, multilayer HEA coatings will accumulate less time-dependent plastic deformation than monolithic HEA coatings.
TEM will reveal dislocation pile-ups or arrested dislocations at multilayer interfaces.
Monolithic HEA coatings without engineered multilayer interfaces will show greater creep strain under the same conditions.
Dislocation-mediated mechanisms can govern time-dependent plastic deformation in HEAs.
At sufficiently high temperatures, thermal activation can overcome interface barriers and reduce the effectiveness of the multilayer design.
At extreme stresses, interface barriers become less effective at resisting creep.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction may vary with processing conditions.
Using compositionally similar adjoining layers will minimize interfacial mismatch.
Temperature-variation creep tests can be used to estimate the activation energy for creep.
Failure of mismatch-rich multilayers to show a statistically significant creep-rate reduction relative to monolithic controls would falsify the proposed interface-governed creep-resistance mechanism.
Absence of dislocation pile-ups or arrested dislocations at interfaces would falsify the proposed dislocation-blocking mechanism.
